Recognise member supply of synthetic graphite (anode-grade), rare-earth oxides & compounds, natural graphite and 7 others in procurement and content rules. Bind market access among members for cobalt intermediates & chemicals and nickel intermediates & chemicals.
Give Minerals Security Partnership and its successor FORGE a compact mandate: pipeline, reciprocal commitments, KPIs and an annual review. No new body.

Do not co-subsidise new PGMs (iridium, ruthenium) capacity among members. Do not run parallel national subsidy races for copper ores & concentrates. Do not create a new compact secretariat or treaty body.

Of 16 electro-industrial nodes in the compact, 15 show an active compact relation (member supply meeting member need, a capacity-constrained trusted supplier or a shared chokepoint), 1 member competition and 0 no strategic case. Nearly every step is under stress, so a compact is the right scale of response; the rules then rank where it acts first (8 nodes need new capacity, the rest coordinated trade).

A coercive supplier holds at least 50% of world supply at 8 nodes: synthetic graphite (anode-grade) (CHN 94%); rare-earth oxides & compounds (CHN 84%); cobalt intermediates & chemicals (CHN 76%); natural graphite (CHN 82%); rare-earth ores (monazite) (CHN 59%); rare-earth metals (CHN 84%); lithium chemicals (CHN 74%); copper smelting & refining (CHN 50%).
AIB node classes under the China shock: BUILD 8, INSUFFICIENT DATA 2, LOW INTERVENTION 6; allied demand across the compact's nodes US$115.7bn.

43 member economies; core (AIB): Chile (resource supplier (SC-GRID)); Japan (specialized technology supplier (SC-GRID)); DR Congo (processing anchor (SC-GRID)); United States (resource supplier (SC-BATTERIES)); Korea (specialized technology supplier (SC-SEMIS)); India (processing anchor (SC-INDUSTRY)); Peru (resource supplier (SC-GRID)); Germany (demand anchor (SC-BATTERIES)).

By 2024 trade, the largest member suppliers (Chile, Peru, Indonesia, Australia and 13 others) supply synthetic graphite (anode-grade), rare-earth oxides & compounds, cobalt intermediates & chemicals, natural graphite, manganese dioxide (EMD) and 9 others, and the largest member buyers are Japan, United States, Korea, Brazil and 14 others; no node is a shared vulnerability that no member can supply.

The trade is market access and demand certainty for trusted capacity: suppliers commit capacity and priority supply, buyers commit offtake and procurement recognition, and the compact keeps the remaining nodes open.

Do not co-subsidise new PGMs (iridium, ruthenium) capacity among members: Germany and South Africa are already strong suppliers. Trusted supply is adequate: this is commercial competition.
Do not run parallel national subsidy races for copper ores & concentrates: 3 members (Chile, DR Congo and Peru) are already strong suppliers; agree in the compact who expands where.
Do not create a new compact secretariat or treaty body: Minerals Security Partnership and its successor FORGE already exists (finance and projects but no published list); dock the compact in it.

. Gaps: CCRM-M1 has no published project pipeline; CCRM-M1 has no dedicated finance; CCRM-M1 has no KPI dashboard or review cycle; core members outside CCRM-M1: CHL, COD, PER.

Do not create a new compact body. Give Minerals Security Partnership and its successor FORGE a compact mandate for these nodes: a shared project pipeline, reciprocal supplier and buyer commitments and a KPI dashboard, reviewed every 12 months.

This section sets out what already exists before anything new is proposed. Facts are from the curated evidence layer (accessed 2026-11-13); items marked partial rest on secondary sources and should be confirmed before citation; unverified items are left out here and stay in the evidence register.

Members in OSI's economic-security agreements table: G7 8 (CAN, DEU, EUU, FRA, GBR, ITA, JPN and USA); IPEF 11 (AUS, IDN, IND, JPN, KOR, MYS, PHL, SGP, THA, USA and VNM); MSP 14 (AUS, CAN, DEU, EUU, FIN, FRA, GBR, IND, ITA, JPN, KOR, NOR and 2 others); MSP Forum 7 (ARG, COD, MEX, NAM, PER, PHL and TUR); NATO 17 (BEL, BGR, CAN, DEU, ESP, FIN, FRA, GBR, GRC, HUN, ITA, NLD and 5 others); U.S. FTA 9 (AUS, CAN, CHL, COL, KOR, MAR, MEX, PER and SGP).

Korean and Japanese officials agreed a close cooperation system on critical-mineral supply risks, support for company and agency cooperation on joint development in third countries (Latin America, Asia, Africa), and policy coordination in the Minerals Security Partnership and IEA; no projects were named.

G7 leaders adopted the plan at Kananaskis on 17 Jun 2025, under Canada's presidency. It tasks ministers with a roadmap for standards-based markets with traceability by year-end, calls on export credit agencies, DFIs and MDBs to scale up mining finance, and targets processing, recycling and substitution R&D. Australia, India and Korea later endorsed it.

Announced in Toronto on 31 Oct 2025, this is the first round of the Production Alliance under the June 2025 G7 Critical Minerals Action Plan. Its 26 investments, partnerships and measures with France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Norway, the US, Australia and Ukraine aim to unlock C$6.4bn (about US$4.6bn at 0.71 USD/CAD) of graphite, rare-earth and scandium projects. They include Government of Canada offtakes with Nouveau Monde Graphite and Rio Tinto (scandium) and up to C$20.2m for joint R&D. Canada also released a roadmap for standards-based critical-minerals markets.

Adopted in Toronto on 31 Oct 2025 as an early action under the Action Plan, it aims to reduce and eventually eliminate dependence on supply chains dominated by non-market practices. It prioritises interoperable traceability systems aligned with the UN Transparency Protocol and lists price floors, procurement, tax and trade measures as tools members may use, with no deadlines.

Carney launched the Alliance at Kananaskis to use strategic investments and offtakes to bring critical-mineral projects into production for defence and advanced technology. At the 30-31 Oct 2025 Toronto ministerial, ministers agreed their critical-minerals envoys would advance the work, and Canada announced investments including offtakes with two Canadian projects. Member list, deal count, values and the US role are not stated in either source.

The second round discussed a joint response to falling copper treatment and refining charges, cooperation within the Minerals Security Partnership and ways to develop critical minerals jointly in third countries; no agreement or named project was reported.

The 4 Feb 2026 Critical Minerals Ministerial at the State Department drew 55 foreign delegations and produced 13 bilateral critical-minerals frameworks or MOUs. These include a framework with Argentina, an agreement with the UK and a US-Mexico action plan proposing border-adjusted price floors, with details due within 60 days; the source does not name the other signatories. Vice President Vance proposed a plurilateral preferential trade zone with reference prices at each production stage, enforced by adjustable tariffs, and FORGE replaced the MSP.

At the 19 Feb 2026 Ministerial, IEA ministers endorsed an expanded phase of the Critical Minerals Security Programme, which was established in 2022. The expansion covers: support for members that set up or expand stockpiles; rapid market assessments and coordinated responses during supply disruptions; regular table-top exercises (a rare-earth exercise was held in Nov 2025); a wider information dashboard; a new Technology Collaboration Programme on recycling and substitution. The release gives no budget.

At PDAC on 2 Mar 2026 Canada announced a second round of 30 partnerships and investments with 12 allied partners, covering C$12.1bn (about US$8.6bn at 0.71 USD/CAD) of projects. This brings the Alliance total to C$18.5bn of Canadian critical-minerals projects. The release does not name the partners or the projects.

VaultCo said on 23 Sep 2026 that Swiss-based traders Glencore and Mercuria had each committed US$500m, and the reserve moved into its operating phase. It is separate from the DLA-run National Defense Stockpile. No mineral purchases, EXIM loan closing, purchase-pricing rules or price-floor mechanism had been disclosed by mid-October 2026. The reported scope is the 60-mineral USGS list, with initial emphasis on rare earths, cobalt, nickel, lithium, copper, gallium, germanium and scandium.
7 further items are in the evidence register (compact_evidence.csv).

ASM made its first commercial sale of terbium and dysprosium from its Korean plant in Jul 2025, to a Neo Performance Materials subsidiary; the buyer is not a Korean firm per the source; day approximate.

Excluding rare earths, the top refining country's average share of key energy minerals rose to 72% in 2025 from 70% in 2023. China is the top refiner of each key energy mineral except nickel, where Indonesia leads. The number of mineral tariff codes under Chinese export controls has tripled since 2023. Full implementation of the expanded rare-earth controls could put about US$6.5 trillion a year of downstream production outside China at risk; a full disruption of battery-grade graphite trade would put over US$300bn a year at risk.

New refining projects in the US and Malaysia cut China's share of rare-earth refining to about 85% in 2025 from 90% in 2023; it could fall to about 70% by 2035 if all planned projects proceed (IEA figures as reported by Reuters). The executive summary adds that diversified refining capacity by 2035 equals about two-thirds of expected mined supply, while planned magnet production equals only about one-third. Diversifying magnet rare-earth supply would need about US$60bn of investment over a decade.

Wesfarmers' 2026 Annual Report (year to 30 Jun 2026) says the Covalent Lithium Kwinana refinery, a Wesfarmers-SQM joint venture, achieved first lithium hydroxide production and sales in FY2026 and is still ramping up. Production rates are expected to accelerate through January-June 2027 as odour mitigation is put in place, while product qualification with key offtake partners continues. No US offtaker or investor is named.

At the 2 Sep 2026 AKBC-KABC meeting in Adelaide POSCO's chair said Australia supplies about 70% of the group's raw materials, as it has since 1971; POSCO also owns Senex Energy (2022); no new agreements were signed.

The Matawinie mine has been under construction since 2026 (C$67m spent by 30 Sep 2026; mining lease granted Oct 2026), and the 13 ktpy Becancour anode plant is targeting FID in the coming months. Offtakers for about 70% of output are Panasonic Energy, Traxys and the Government of Canada, and the Canada Growth Fund committed about US$82m in Apr 2026; no US buyer or US government finance is named.

Signed 28 Mar 2023 and in force on signature without congressional approval; covers cobalt/graphite/lithium/manganese/nickel; no export duties; consult on non-market measures and forced-labour imports; Treasury/USTR treated it as an FTA for the IRA EV credit critical-minerals test.

Albanese and Trump signed the US-Australia Framework for Securing of Supply in the Mining and Processing of Critical Minerals and Rare Earths in Washington on 20 Oct 2025. Each side is to provide at least US$1bn within six months toward an US$8.5bn pipeline of priority projects, and a Supply Security Response Group led by the US Energy Secretary and the Australian Resources Minister is to be set up. Japan is not a party.

Trump and Takaichi signed a framework on 2025-10-28 in Tokyo covering permitting streamlining, coordinated investment and a Supply Security Rapid Response Group led by the US Energy Secretary and Japan's METI minister.

Under the 26 Oct 2025 US-Malaysia reciprocal trade agreement, Malaysia agreed not to ban or impose quotas on exports of critical minerals or rare earths to the US. On 29 Oct 2025 its trade minister said the January 2024 ban on raw rare-earth exports remains, so rare earths must be processed in Malaysia before export.

The White House says China will suspend the global implementation of the export controls it announced on 9 Oct 2025. It also says China will issue general licences for exports of rare earths, gallium, germanium, antimony and graphite to US end users and their suppliers worldwide, which it calls the de facto removal of controls China has imposed since 2023.

The final 2025 list, published on 7 Nov 2025, has 60 minerals, up from 50 in 2022. It adds boron, copper, lead, metallurgical coal, phosphate, potash, rhenium, silicon, silver and uranium. The list is to be updated not less than every two years.

On 9 Nov 2025 MOFCOM suspended clause 2 of Announcement No. 46 of 2024 until 27 Nov 2026. That clause barred, in principle, exports to the US of gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard-material dual-use items, and subjected graphite exports to stricter end-user and end-use checks; licensing still applies. No extension of this suspension was reported as of 13 Nov 2026.

The 14 Jan 2026 Section 232 proclamation imposes no tariffs. It directs Commerce and USTR to negotiate agreements with trading partners and to promote price floors for trade in processed critical minerals and derivative products. Further import measures may follow if agreements are not reached within 180 days (about 13 Jul 2026), are not carried out or prove ineffective. The fact sheet cites no import-dependence figures.

On 31 Oct 2025 Canada said it would use the Defence Production Act to stockpile critical minerals. The stated purposes are domestic and allied defence supply, Arctic sovereignty and NATO goals. The Defence Industrial Strategy of 17 Feb 2026 allows stockpiling of critical and dual-use minerals. Volumes and budget are not stated.

Proclamation 10962 (30 Jul 2025) imposed a 50% tariff on the copper content of semi-finished copper products and intensive derivatives from 1 Aug 2025. It does not stack on Section 232 auto tariffs. A refined-copper duty of 15% from 1 Jan 2027 and 30% from 1 Jan 2028 depended on a Commerce market update due 30 Jun 2026, and no decision on it was reported.

Proclamation 11021 (2 Apr 2026) set full-value Section 232 duties of 50% on steel, aluminium and certain copper articles, with lower UK rates only. For the Annex I-C derivative list, Proclamation 11032 charges USMCA-qualifying Canadian and Mexican products 25% on non-US content only (floor 15%), while Japan, Korea, the EU, the UK and others receive a 15% all-in cap that Canada does not.

On 9 Oct 2026 the Commission selected 46 strategic projects in 16 member states: 7 on lithium, 12 nickel, 10 cobalt, 5 manganese, 4 graphite and 4 rare earths. They add to 47 EU and 13 third-country projects chosen in 2025. Since the Dec 2025 RESourceEU communication, Team Europe has committed over EUR 2bn through the Innovation Fund, state aid and the EIB, and the Raw Materials Mechanism has made over 30 matches for 10 materials. No US company or US-located project is named.

Announcement 2026 No. 58 of 9 Nov 2026 keeps MOFCOM/GAC Announcements 2025 Nos. 55, 56, 57 and 58 and MOFCOM Announcements 2025 Nos. 61 and 62 suspended from 11 Nov 2026 to 10 Jan 2027. These are the October 2025 controls on superhard materials, rare-earth equipment, further medium and heavy rare earths, lithium-battery and graphite-anode items, the extraterritorial rare-earth rule and rare-earth technology. The extension adds two months to the Busan-truce suspension, which was due to lapse on 10 Nov 2026. China's April 2025 licensing of seven medium and heavy rare earths (UJ-024) is not part of the suspension.
5 further items are in the evidence register (compact_evidence.csv).

Announced on 9 Jan 2020 after a June 2019 leaders' commitment, the plan covers industry engagement, supply chains for strategic industries and defence, sharing information on mineral resources, cooperation in multilateral forums, joint R&D and supply-chain modelling. The release names no funding, targets or review dates, and its current status is not stated in any 2025-26 source.

TRUST (Transforming the Relationship Utilizing Strategic Technology) covers AI, semiconductors, quantum, biotech, energy and space and commits to trusted supply chains for semiconductors and critical minerals. Under it the leaders launched the Strategic Mineral Recovery initiative to recover and process lithium, cobalt and rare earths from aluminium, coal-mining and oil-and-gas streams; no budget or project list is given.

Signed in Kuala Lumpur on 26 Oct 2025, the non-binding MOU commits both sides to coordinate support for bilateral projects and to prioritise US investment in Malaysian critical-minerals assets offered for sale. It also commits them to strengthen review of rare-earth asset sales and to protect both markets through high-standard marketplaces under a pricing framework that includes price floors or similar measures. Working-level meetings are to be quarterly, and no funds are obligated.

Signed in Kuala Lumpur on 26 Oct 2025, the MOU gives the Participants an expected first opportunity to invest in critical-minerals assets offered for sale in Thailand or by Thai companies. It provides for early sharing of tender information, US help in assessing Thailand's resource base, technology transfer, priority for domestic processing and national-security review of rare-earth asset sales. Both sides will trade preferentially in high-standard marketplaces under a pricing framework that includes price floors or similar measures.

The US and the DRC signed a Strategic Partnership Agreement alongside the December 2025 Washington peace accords. The State Department says its core objectives are more US investment in DRC mining and secure copper and cobalt flows to the United States. The text, any list of assets offered and the exact signing date (reported as 4 Dec 2025) are not confirmed in a primary source.

At the 4 Feb 2026 ministerial (54 countries and the European Commission), the US signed 11 bilateral critical-minerals frameworks or MOUs: Argentina, Cook Islands, Ecuador, Guinea, Morocco, Paraguay, Peru, the Philippines, the UAE, the UK and Uzbekistan. These add to 10 signed in the previous five months, with negotiations concluded with 17 more countries; the frameworks cover pricing, development, supply gaps and access to finance. FORGE, chaired by Korea through June 2026, replaced the Minerals Security Partnership.

Announced on 24 Apr 2026 as the primary US-EU mechanism for coordinating trade measures on critical-minerals supply chains, 'with a view to concluding a binding plurilateral agreement on trade in critical minerals'. The parties will examine tools including border-adjusted price floors; the release names no minerals, price levels or deadlines. The plan accompanies the State Department-Commission MOU of the same day (USDE-09).

The EU has raw-materials partnership memoranda with 17 partners. They include Argentina (13 Jun 2023), Chile (18 Jul 2023), the DRC and Zambia (26 Oct 2023), Norway (21 Mar 2024), Australia (28 May 2024), Canada (2021), South Africa (20 Nov 2025), the United States (24 Apr 2026) and New Caledonia (20 Oct 2026). They rest on letters of intent or political frameworks, with no binding volumes or finance.

Signed on 4 Dec 2025 and tied to peace in eastern DRC, the agreement creates a Strategic Asset Reserve: a list of Congolese mining assets on which US companies get preferential access. The IEA summary adds a right of first offer on minerals marketed for export to US persons. The steering committee met on 5 Feb 2026, when the first asset list was designated, and in Paris on 5 Nov 2026. At the Paris meeting the SAR legal framework was still not final, and DFC presented DRC investments in preparation without figures.

On 13 Dec 2024 the US DoD awarded US$15.8m under DPA Title III to take the Yukon Mactung tungsten project toward a final investment decision, and Canada's CMIF offered up to C$12.9m for road and power planning (C$35.4m combined; the CMIF agreement was signed 27 Aug 2025). A feasibility study began on 9 Mar 2026, and JX Advanced Metals took a strategic stake in a C$61.5m placement closed on 2 Apr 2026.

Syrah's 11.25 ktpa Vidalia plant began AAM production in February 2024 from Balama (Mozambique) graphite. It is backed by a US$102m DOE loan (binding July 2022), a Tesla offtake (December 2021), a Lucid offtake (February 2025) and a US$165m 48C credit (January 2025). The credit supports a 45 ktpa expansion whose FID depends on financing. Syrah describes itself as the only operating vertically integrated natural-graphite AAM supplier outside China.
DoD bought $400M of Series A convertible preferred (7% PIK dividend) and extended a $150M 12-year unsecured samarium project loan; closing was set for 2025-07-11.

Australia offered up to US$200m concessional equity with an offtake right and the US also takes equity with an offtake right; trilateral with Japan, which has funded 50% of costs; could supply up to 10% of world gallium.

Under a five-year offtake signed 8 Dec 2025, REalloys will buy most of the NdPr metal and Dy/Tb oxide output of SRC's Saskatoon facility (400 t/yr NdPr metal rising to 600 t/yr; full operation expected early 2027) for US defence clients. On 12 Mar 2026 REalloys announced a heavy-rare-earth metallization facility to be built in Saskatoon and later moved to Ohio, taking 80% of the output.

Deputy Secretary Landau witnessed an MOU between Glencore and the US-backed Orion Critical Mineral Consortium on a potential acquisition of assets in the DRC. State says the deal reflects the US-DRC Strategic Partnership Agreement's aim of copper and cobalt flows to the United States. The assets, stake and price are not named.

Redwood has received more than 28,000 t of material for recycling from GM and Ultium Cells (GM's joint venture with LG Energy Solution), and about 10,000 GM EV packs are in the pipeline for repurposing through Redwood Energy. Its second-life system in Sparks, Nevada serves AI firm Crusoe, and a 1.5 MW/7.2 MWh repurposed-pack installation is planned at a GM plant in Michigan.

On 11 Jun 2026 NOVONIX delivered a mass-production qualification (C-) sample of synthetic graphite AAM from Chattanooga to its lead customer Panasonic Energy; the company calls it the first such sample made in North America. It expects mass production for Panasonic in H2 2027, subject to qualification. The release does not mention the status of its DOE conditional loan.

KfW's Raw Materials Fund (part of the Germany Fund) made its first two equity decisions, EUR 150m in Vulcan Energy (lithium) and EUR 50m in Arafura's Nolans rare earths project; a third is in due diligence and the target size is EUR 1.5bn; no US-linked project named; USD at about 1.16 per EUR.
POSCO's 4 Sep 2026 release says it acquired a stake in a high-quality lithium mine owned by Mineral Resources in 2026; mine name, stake size and amount are not given.

Since the RESourceEU communication of December 2025, Team Europe has committed more than EUR 2bn (about US$2.3bn at 1.16 USD/EUR) through the Innovation Fund, State aid and the EIB. The Raw Materials Mechanism, which aggregates demand and matches offtakers, has produced more than 30 matches for 10 materials. Of the 2025 Strategic Projects, 25 have completed environmental assessment and 17 hold construction permits.

Lynas's quarterly report of 29 Oct 2026 describes its growth programme as the heavy rare earths expansion and JS Link magnet plant in Malaysia, supply to JS Link in Korea, an LS Eco Energy metal plant in Vietnam and the proposed Meteoric (Brazil) acquisition announced on 1 Oct 2026. The report does not mention the Seadrift, Texas plant, and no construction start has been announced. Floor-price agreements now cover over 50% of Lynas production.

On 31 Mar 2026 Export Finance Australia signed a binding subscription for US$100m (about A$146m) of Arafura equity, alongside about A$84m from KfW for Germany's Raw Material Fund. Shareholders re-approved the issue on 22 Oct 2026, and both subscriptions are expected to complete when the Nolans project debt reaches contractual close.

Arafura took FID on Nolans on 21 May 2026. Early construction works began in the September 2026 quarter, about A$700m of procurement scope was advanced, and a ground-breaking ceremony was held after 30 Sep. The export credit agency and commercial lender group, which the report does not name, is completing final credit approvals for contractual close of the project debt.

After 30 Sep 2026, Arafura signed a binding five-year offtake for Nolans NdPr with a US trading group named as a Project Vault participant, with volumes rising to 850 t/yr once the project reaches nameplate production. Arafura no longer names offtake counterparties and expects its remaining uncommitted NdPr to come from the 500 t/yr earmarked under Australia's Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve. The exact signing date is not stated in the report.

The DoD awarded US$20m under DPA Title III on 19 Aug 2024, noting Canada's eligibility for Title III funds. As of 9 Nov 2026 the ~C$100m (US$73m) build is on budget with C$59.3m of government contributions (including a C$20m federal agreement of 4 May 2026 and C$17.5m from Ontario); early commissioning is targeted for Q4 2026 and commercial production for 2H 2027, at 5,120 t/yr contained cobalt, with about 60% committed to LG Energy Solution.

The DRC suspended cobalt exports on 22 Feb 2025 and replaced the ban with ARECOMS-allocated quotas from 16 Oct 2025. The quotas were reported as 18,125 t for the rest of 2025 and 96,600 t a year for 2026 and 2027, with part held back as a strategic quota. These volumes come from press reports, not the ARECOMS decision.

Under the 26 Oct 2025 US-Malaysia reciprocal trade agreement, Malaysia agreed not to ban or impose quotas on exports of critical minerals or rare earths to the US. On 29 Oct 2025 its trade minister said the January 2024 ban on raw rare-earth exports remains, so rare earths must be processed in Malaysia before export.

The White House says China will suspend the global implementation of the export controls it announced on 9 Oct 2025. It also says China will issue general licences for exports of rare earths, gallium, germanium, antimony and graphite to US end users and their suppliers worldwide, which it calls the de facto removal of controls China has imposed since 2023.

On 9 Nov 2025 MOFCOM suspended clause 2 of Announcement No. 46 of 2024 until 27 Nov 2026. That clause barred, in principle, exports to the US of gallium, germanium, antimony and superhard-material dual-use items, and subjected graphite exports to stricter end-user and end-use checks; licensing still applies. No extension of this suspension was reported as of 13 Nov 2026.

The 14 Jan 2026 Section 232 proclamation imposes no tariffs. It directs Commerce and USTR to negotiate agreements with trading partners and to promote price floors for trade in processed critical minerals and derivative products. Further import measures may follow if agreements are not reached within 180 days (about 13 Jul 2026), are not carried out or prove ineffective. The fact sheet cites no import-dependence figures.

Proclamation 10962 (30 Jul 2025) imposed a 50% tariff on the copper content of semi-finished copper products and intensive derivatives from 1 Aug 2025. It does not stack on Section 232 auto tariffs. A refined-copper duty of 15% from 1 Jan 2027 and 30% from 1 Jan 2028 depended on a Commerce market update due 30 Jun 2026, and no decision on it was reported.

Proclamation 11021 (2 Apr 2026) set full-value Section 232 duties of 50% on steel, aluminium and certain copper articles, with lower UK rates only. For the Annex I-C derivative list, Proclamation 11032 charges USMCA-qualifying Canadian and Mexican products 25% on non-US content only (floor 15%), while Japan, Korea, the EU, the UK and others receive a 15% all-in cap that Canada does not.

Announcement 2026 No. 58 of 9 Nov 2026 keeps MOFCOM/GAC Announcements 2025 Nos. 55, 56, 57 and 58 and MOFCOM Announcements 2025 Nos. 61 and 62 suspended from 11 Nov 2026 to 10 Jan 2027. These are the October 2025 controls on superhard materials, rare-earth equipment, further medium and heavy rare earths, lithium-battery and graphite-anode items, the extraterritorial rare-earth rule and rare-earth technology. The extension adds two months to the Busan-truce suspension, which was due to lapse on 10 Nov 2026. China's April 2025 licensing of seven medium and heavy rare earths (UJ-024) is not part of the suspension.

Syrah's 11.25 ktpa Vidalia plant began AAM production in February 2024 from Balama (Mozambique) graphite. It is backed by a US$102m DOE loan (binding July 2022), a Tesla offtake (December 2021), a Lucid offtake (February 2025) and a US$165m 48C credit (January 2025). Excluding rare earths, the top refining country's average share of key energy minerals rose to 72% in 2025 from 70% in 2023. China is the top refiner of each key energy mineral except nickel, where Indonesia leads. The number of mineral tariff codes under Chinese export controls has tripled since 2023. Full implementation of the expanded rare-earth controls could put about US$6.5 trillion a year of downstream production outside China at risk; a full disruption of battery-grade graphite trade would put over US$300bn a year at risk.

No US offtaker or investor is named.
POSCO's 4 Sep 2026 release says it acquired a stake in a high-quality lithium mine owned by Mineral Resources in 2026; mine name, stake size and amount are not given.

The export credit agency and commercial lender group, which the report does not name, is completing final credit approvals for contractual close of the project debt.
